questions.q: State the closure property of rational numbers under subtraction that is used in this proof.
questions.a: If a and b are rational numbers, then a − b is also rational. A wrong answer (e.g., "rational minus irrational is rational") reveals the student confuses closure (which applies only to operations within the rationals) with cross-set operations.

questions.q: In the proof, after assuming 5 − √3 = r (rational), we write √3 = 5 − r. Explain why this step is valid and why it leads to a contradiction.
questions.a: The step is valid because we simply rearranged the equation (subtracted r from both sides, then swapped). Since 5 is rational and r is rational (by assumption), 5 − r is rational by closure. But this says √3 is rational, contradicting the proven fact that √3 is irrational. A wrong answer (e.g., "we assumed √3 is irrational so it stays irrational") misses that the contradiction arises from the assumption, not from an independent fact.

questions.q: Give the correct order of steps in the contradiction proof that 5 minus √3 is irrational.
questions.a: The proof runs: (1) Assume 5 minus √3 equals a rational number r (2) Rearrange to get √3 equals 5 minus r (3) Closure under subtraction makes 5 minus r rational (4) This contradicts the proven irrationality of √3, so the assumption fails. A wrong answer that accepts the slogan that rational and irrational never mix as a proof shows the student has missed that the assertion needs the contradiction argument, not intuition.

questions.q: Is 5 + √3 irrational? Prove it using the same method.
questions.a: Yes. Assume 5 + √3 = r (rational). Then √3 = r − 5. Since r and 5 are rational, r − 5 is rational, so √3 is rational — contradiction. Hence 5 + √3 is irrational. A wrong answer (e.g., "yes, because addition works the same way") without the proof shows the student recognises the pattern but cannot formalise it.

questions.q: Is √3 − 5 irrational? How does this differ from 5 − √3?
questions.a: Yes, √3 − 5 is irrational. Proof: assume √3 − 5 = r (rational). Then √3 = r + 5. Since r and 5 are rational, r + 5 is rational, so √3 is rational — contradiction. It differs from 5 − √3 only in sign; both are irrational because the irrational component √3 cannot be eliminated by adding/subtracting a rational. A wrong answer (e.g., "√3 − 5 = −(5 − √3) so it's rational if 5 − √3 is rational") confuses negation with rationality — the negative of an irrational is still irrational.

questions.q: Prove that 7 − 2√5 is irrational. (Hint: Use the irrationality of √5 and closure of rationals.)
questions.a: Assume 7 − 2√5 = r (rational). Then 2√5 = 7 − r. Since 7 and r are rational, 7 − r is rational, so 2√5 is rational. Then √5 = (7 − r)/2, which is rational (division of rational by non-zero rational 2). But √5 is irrational (proved similarly to √3). Contradiction. Hence 7 − 2√5 is irrational. A poor answer fails to handle the coefficient 2 correctly or forgets that √5 must be proven or assumed irrational.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: This is proved by ______ using the sum/difference property: the sum or difference of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number is always irrational.
Fill in the blank: We also know that rational numbers are closed under addition and ______: if you subtract two rationals, you get a rational.
Fill in the blank: If √______ becomes a difference of two rationals, it must be rational — contradicting what we already proved.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently prove that 5 − √3 is irrational by assuming the contrary, isolating √3, and invoking the closure of rationals under subtraction along with the known irrationality of √3 to derive a contradiction.
